reply: It started three days ago with a dry, hacking cough, and I have been burning up on and off, roasting even without a thermometer. Since yesterday, I am bringing stuff up that changed from clear to a rusty, brownish colour, and a sharp pain started low down on the right side round towards my back that catches me when I take a deep breath or cough.

utterance: Thanks. A few more questions: Are you short of breath at all — at rest, or when walking around the house? Have you had any shaking chills or rigors? And have you coughed up any blood?
reply: I only get puffed going up the stairs or on the way in from the car park, but sitting here I am alright. The first night I was shaking under the doona with my teeth chattering, even though I was boiling. I have not coughed up any actual blood, just that rusty colour. Paracetamol for fever and chest pain

utterance:
Mark, here's what's going on. Your examination and the chest X-ray show you have pneumonia — a bacterial infection in the lower part of your right lung. That explains the fever, shaking chills, rusty-coloured phlegm, and the sharp pain when you breathe in, which is the lining of the lung being irritated. The good news is that your oxygen level, blood pressure and pulse are all reasonable, you're alert and drinking well, and you're otherwise healthy, so this is safe to treat at home with tablets rather than in hospital.

The plan:
1. Antibiotics: amoxicillin, 2 capsules (1 gram) three times a day for 7 days. Take the first dose as soon as you get them. Finish the whole course even when you feel better.
2. Paracetamol, 2 tablets up to four times a day (no more than 8 tablets in 24 hours) for the fever and the chest pain — it'll also make it easier to take deep breaths and cough the phlegm up, which helps the lung clear.
3. Rest, keep drinking plenty of fluids, and stay off work — you'll need at least this week off, and I'll give you a medical certificate. Please don't go back to the classroom until the fever has settled and you're feeling stronger.
4. I've sent off blood tests, a phlegm sample and a nose swab for viruses including COVID and flu. I'll call you with results in a day or two.
5. Review: I want to see you again in 48 hours — the day after tomorrow — to check you're improving. You should notice the fever easing within 2 to 3 days. If it hasn't, we may need to change the antibiotic.

Very important — go straight to the emergency department or call 000 if any of these happen: you become short of breath at rest or when talking, your lips or fingers look blue, you get confused or very drowsy, you cough up actual blood, the fever climbs and the shaking chills return despite the antibiotics, you can't keep fluids or the tablets down, you're passing very little urine, or the chest pain becomes severe or sudden. Don't wait for the appointment if you're getting worse.

Also, once you're well, I'd recommend getting your flu vaccine each year. Does all of that make sense, and do you have any questions?
reply: Pneumonia? Well, that explains why I have been feeling so rotten, though I am glad I can stay at home rather than go into hospital. I had better let the school know I am out for the week.

utterance: Good plan — let the school know you're off this week. I'll print your medical certificate and the prescriptions now. Book in with reception for the review in two days, and remember: if you get worse before then, especially with breathlessness, confusion or worsening fever, don't wait — go to the emergency department. Take care, Mark, and rest up.
reply: Thanks, Doc. I will go and get these tablets sorted.
